name: Puerarin (kudzu root compound)
short: Puerarin injection: 129 published adverse-reaction cases (mostly immune or blood), 13 deaths; trial reviews: none serious (stroke), rates like control (heart failure). No by-mouth safety data found.
text: All the safety sources found concern puerarin given by injection (intravenous infusion), which is widely used in China; no safety data on puerarin taken by mouth were found. A review of published reports collected 129 cases of adverse reactions to puerarin injection from 62 papers: most involved the immune and blood systems (88.3%), most were moderate or severe (64.3%), and 13 of the 129 cases died; these are counts of reported cases, so they do not show how often harm occurs, and the authors advised asking about allergy history before use. A laboratory study notes that adverse reactions, especially haemolysis (destruction of red blood cells) in the vein, have limited clinical use of the injection, and found that puerarin broke down human red blood cells at high concentrations in saline. In contrast, meta-analyses of randomised trials reported no serious reactions in stroke and similar reaction rates in heart failure: in 35 trials (3,224 participants) in acute ischaemic stroke, 11 trials reported facial flushing, dizziness, vomiting, nausea, mild stomach discomfort and allergic reactions, with no serious reactions, though the authors noted a lack of adequate safety data; in 8 trials (614 patients) in acute heart failure, which tested the injection as an add-on treatment and compared it with conventional medicine alone, adverse reactions occurred in 23 of 194 patients (11.9%) in the injection groups and 19 of 194 (9.8%) in the control groups, not a significant difference; the abstract does not describe the reactions or how severe they were. On interactions, a review reported that puerarin injection altered the effect of anticoagulant drugs through CYP enzymes, pharmacokinetics and blood-flow measures, but concluded it is difficult to say whether such herbal medicines increase or reduce the effects of anticoagulant or antiplatelet drugs.
